fields.objective: Difference between large / small scale map
enabling_objectives: Define large scale map and small scale map using ratio notation
Identify whether a given map is large scale or small scale based on its numerical ratio
Compare the level of detail shown on a large scale map versus a small scale map
Determine which type of map (large or small scale) is appropriate for a given geographic task or region
Calculate the actual ground distance from a measurement on a large scale map using its scale bar or ratio
Calculate the actual ground distance from a measurement on a small scale map using its scale bar or ratio
Explain how map scale affects the area coverage and geographic accuracy represented on a map

fields.title: Give direction on maps both as compass point and bearing
fields.objective: Give direction on maps both as compass point and bearing

dropped_examples.rejected_eo: Identify the eight cardinal and intercardinal compass points on a map or diagram; Read a compass bearing measured clockwise from north in degrees (0–360°)

enabling_objectives: Identify the eight cardinal and intercardinal compass points on a map or diagram
Read a compass bearing measured clockwise from north in degrees (0–360°)
Convert a compass point direction (e.g., NE, SW) to its equivalent bearing in degrees
Convert a bearing in degrees to its equivalent compass point direction
Measure the bearing between two locations on a map using a protractor or compass rose
Describe the direction from one map location to another using both compass points and bearings
Apply bearing and compass direction conventions to solve a navigation problem on a map

fields.title: Calculate coordinate systems on maps using the reference ...
fields.objective: Calculate coordinate systems on maps using the reference system (four-figure and six-figure grid references)
enabling_objectives: Identify the grid squares on a map using row and column labels
Read a four-figure grid reference from a map to locate a specific square
Construct a four-figure grid reference for a given location on a map
Read a six-figure grid reference from a map to pinpoint a precise location within a square
Construct a six-figure grid reference by subdividing a grid square and estimating position
Convert between four-figure and six-figure grid reference systems for the same location
Solve a navigation problem by calculating the distance between two map locations using grid references

fields.title: Measure distances along straight and curved distances
fields.objective: Measure distances along straight and curved distances
enabling_objectives: Read a scale on a map to determine the ground distance it represents
Measure a straight-line distance on a map using a ruler
Convert a measured map distance to actual ground distance using the map scale
Measure a curved distance on a map using a string or tracing method
Apply the map scale to convert a curved measurement into actual ground distance
Compare straight-line distance versus actual path distance on a route
Solve a navigation problem by calculating total distance along a marked route

fields.title: Give brief descriptions of landscape using geographical t...
fields.objective: Give brief descriptions of landscape using geographical terms (e.g. plains, gently-sloping land)
enabling_objectives: Identify plains and flat landforms in a landscape description or diagram
Identify gently-sloping land in a landscape description or diagram
Identify steep slopes and mountainous terrain in a landscape description or diagram
Match geographical terms (plains, slopes, ridges, valleys) to landscape features in images or text
Describe a landscape using at least three geographical terms in a single paragraph
Classify landscape types (e.g. coastal, mountainous, valley-based) using appropriate geographical vocabulary
Distinguish between gently-sloping and steeply-sloping terrain in comparative landscape descriptions

fields.title: Describe the shape and form of river channel
fields.objective: Describe the shape and form of river channel
enabling_objectives: Identify the cross-sectional profile shape of a river channel (V-shaped, U-shaped, or box-shaped)
Label the width and depth dimensions on a river channel cross-section diagram
Distinguish between the banks, bed, and floodplain in a river channel diagram
Compare the channel shapes found in upper course, middle course, and lower course sections of a river
Relate specific landforms (waterfalls, meanders, deltas) to the characteristic shape of the river channel at that location
Sketch a cross-section of a river channel showing its depth-to-width ratio at a given location
Explain how channel shape changes are caused by erosion and deposition processes

fields.title: Define the term weathering and Mass movements
fields.objective: Define the term weathering and Mass movements
enabling_objectives: Define weathering as the breakdown of rock in situ by physical, chemical, or biological processes
Distinguish between physical weathering, chemical weathering, and biological weathering with examples
Identify causes of physical weathering such as freeze-thaw, exfoliation, and abrasion
Identify causes of chemical weathering such as oxidation, carbonation, and hydrolysis
Define mass movement as the downhill movement of rock and soil under gravity without a transporting agent
Classify types of mass movements including slides, falls, creep, and flows
Explain the relationship between weathering and mass movement in landscape formation

fields.title: Types of weathering physical, chemicals and Biological.
fields.objective: Types of weathering physical, chemicals and Biological.
enabling_objectives: Identify examples of physical weathering processes such as freeze-thaw and exfoliation
Distinguish between physical weathering and chemical weathering based on observable characteristics
Classify given weathering scenarios as physical, chemical, or biological
Explain how chemical weathering alters rock composition through oxidation or acid reactions
Identify biological weathering agents such as plant roots, lichens, and burrowing organisms
Compare the relative rates of physical, chemical, and biological weathering in different climates
Analyze a rock sample or photograph to determine which type of weathering has affected it most

fields.teacher_script: A straight line is flat and continuous—it never bends. When you place a ray (or another line) starting at any point on a straight line, it divides that line into two angles on either side. Since the line is straight, those two angles must fit together perfectly to form the complete flat surface, which is always 180°. Think of it like splitting a perfectly flat piece of sugarcane in half: the two pieces together make the whole.

key_points: A straight line measures 180°.
Any ray from a point on a straight line creates two angles on either side.
These two angles always sum to 180°.
We call these angles supplementary angles.

key_vocabulary.example: The horizon of the ocean.
key_vocabulary.definition: A line that is flat and continuous with no bends, measuring 180°.

key_vocabulary.example: A sunbeam shining from the sun.
key_vocabulary.definition: A line that starts at a point and extends infinitely in one direction.

key_vocabulary.example: Angles of 70° and 110° are supplementary.
key_vocabulary.definition: Two angles that add up to 180°.

educational_content.seychelles_context: The horizon line as seen from any of Seychelles' 115 islands is a perfect straight line of 180°. A lighthouse beam and the horizon line create supplementary angles.

fields.concept_tag: straight_line_angles
fields.enabling_objective: Identify that angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees

fields.teacher_script: Imagine you're standing on the eastern shore of Mahé watching the sun rise and set—the path of the sun across the sky forms a straight line from horizon to horizon. Any angle you measure along that straight-line horizon always adds up to 180 degrees. Today we're learning why angles on any straight line always sum to 180°, and how to use this to find missing angles.

images.caption: Angles on a straight line always add to 180°.
images.alt_text: Horizontal straight line with a ray dividing it into two angles that sum to 180 degrees
images.description: A horizontal straight line with a ray extending upward from a point on the line, creating two angles on either side of the ray. Label the left angle as 'a' and the right angle as 'b'. Mark the straight line with an arrow at each end. Show a = 120° and b = 60° as an example, and label the sum 'a + b = 180°' below the diagram.

fields.concept_tag: straight_line_angles

fields.teacher_script: A common mistake is forgetting that ALL angles on a straight line must sum to 180°, not just two. If you see three or four angles on the same straight line, you still add them all up and set the sum equal to 180°. Another mistake: students sometimes mix up angles on a straight line (180°) with angles around a point (360°). A straight line is only half a full rotation, so it's always 180°, never 360°.

common_mistakes: Only adding two angles when there are three or more angles on the straight line.
Confusing angles on a straight line (180°) with angles around a point (360°).
Forgetting to check the answer by adding all angles to verify they equal 180°.

fields.concept_tag: straight_line_angles
fields.enabling_objective: Identify that angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees

fields.teacher_script: Here's a real-world application from Seychelles. At a market stall in Victoria, a shop owner positions a shade cloth on a straight-line frame.
fields.question: At a market stall in Victoria, a shop owner positions a shade cloth on a straight line frame. The frame is divided by support poles into angles of 28°, 95°, and y. Find y.
fields.hint_1: All angles on the straight frame line must add to 180°.
fields.hint_3: First calculate 28° + 95°, then subtract from 180°.

educational_content.seychelles_context: Market stalls in Victoria often use shade structures with straight frames and support poles that create angles.

fields.concept_tag: straight_line_angles
fields.enabling_objective: Calculate a missing angle on a straight line given one or more other angles

fields.teacher_script: Now let's check your understanding with a true/false question about angles on navigation maps.
fields.question: A straight line on a navigation map is marked with two angle measurements: one angle is three times the other. If the smaller angle is 45°, is the larger angle 135°?
fields.hint_1: If the smaller angle is 45° and the larger is three times bigger, what is 3 × 45°?
fields.hint_2: Calculate: 3 × 45° = 135°
fields.hint_3: Check: 45° + 135° = 180°? This confirms the answer.

educational_content.seychelles_context: Navigation maps of Seychelles' EEZ and the 115 islands often use angle measurements to show compass bearings and routes.

fields.concept_tag: straight_line_angles
fields.enabling_objective: Calculate a missing angle on a straight line given one or more other angles

fields.teacher_script: Let's test your understanding with a multiple choice question. On a straight line, one angle is 28° less than the other.
fields.question: On a straight line, one angle is 28° less than the other. Both angles are on the same straight line. Which pair of angles is correct?
fields.hint_1: Let the smaller angle be x. Then the larger angle is (x + 28°).
fields.hint_2: Set up: x + (x + 28°) = 180°. This simplifies to 2x + 28° = 180°.
fields.hint_3: Solve: 2x = 152°, so x = 76°. The other angle is 76° + 28° = 104°. Check: 76° + 104° = 180° ✓

fields.teacher_script: Imagine a fair lottery in Seychelles where every week, a shop owner draws a winning ticket from a drum. This week, 100 tickets are sold, and your friend has bought 25 of them. What is the probability your friend wins? Today we're going to learn how to predict the number of times an event will happen over many trials — we call this the expected outcome.

images.caption: Probability is the ratio of favourable outcomes to total possible outcomes.
images.alt_text: Lottery drum with 25 winning tickets out of 100 total tickets, showing probability calculation
images.description: A lottery drum with 100 tickets inside, 25 highlighted in red. Below, a label showing 'Probability of winning = 25/100 = 0.25 or 25%'. Include a Seychelles flag and a shop counter setting.

fields.concept_tag: expected_outcome_intro

fields.teacher_script: The expected outcome is what we predict will happen on average when we repeat an event many times. To calculate it, we multiply the probability by the total number of trials: Expected Outcome = Probability × Total Number. For example, if a coin has a 0.5 probability of landing heads, and you flip it 100 times, the expected number of heads is 0.5 × 100 = 50. Think of it like this: if every individual has a 50% chance and you have 100 individuals, roughly 50 will experience that event.

images.caption: The expected outcome formula applies to any event repeated multiple times.
images.alt_text: Formula and three calculation examples for expected outcome
images.description: Formula box showing: Expected Outcome = Probability × Total Number. Below, three worked examples side-by-side: (1) Coin flip: P = 0.5, N = 100, EO = 50; (2) Die roll (rolling a 6): P = 1/6 ≈ 0.167, N = 60, EO = 10; (3) Lottery draw: P = 0.25, N = 40, EO = 10. Label each component clearly.

fields.concept_tag: expected_outcome_concept
fields.enabling_objective: Calculate expected outcome by multiplying probability by total number

fields.teacher_script: Let's work through a complete problem step-by-step. A boat rental business in Seychelles has a 15% chance that each boat will need repairs on any given day. They own 120 boats. How many boats do we expect to need repairs on a typical day?

images.caption: Always extract probability and total number first, then multiply to find expected outcome.
images.alt_text: Flowchart showing step-by-step solution to boat repair expected outcome problem
images.description: Step-by-step worked solution displayed as a flowchart: 'Problem Statement' → 'Extract Probability (15% = 0.15)' → 'Extract Total (120 boats)' → 'Formula: 0.15 × 120' → 'Calculate: 18 boats' → 'Interpretation: 18 boats expected to need repairs'. Use arrows to connect each step.

fields.concept_tag: expected_outcome_concept
fields.enabling_objective: Calculate expected outcome by multiplying probability by total number

fields.teacher_script: Let's work with comparisons. A tourism company is considering two different ferry routes between islands in Seychelles. Route A carries 600 passengers per day with a 2% chance that any passenger will request a refund. Route B carries 400 passengers per day with a 5% chance that any passenger will request a refund. Which route expects more refund requests?
fields.question: A ferry company operates two routes. Route A carries 600 passengers per day with a 2% chance that any passenger will request a refund. Route B carries 400 passengers per day with a 5% chance of a refund. Which route expects more refund requests, and by how many?
choices: A) Route A expects 2 more refund requests than Route B
B) Route B expects 14 more refund requests than Route A
C) Route A expects 14 more refund requests than Route B
D) Both routes expect the same number of refund requests
fields.hint_1: Calculate expected refunds for Route A: 0.02 × 600
fields.hint_2: Calculate expected refunds for Route B: 0.05 × 400
fields.hint_3: Compare the two results and find the difference

images.caption: Comparing expected outcomes requires calculating both values, then finding the difference.
images.alt_text: Comparison of expected refunds for two ferry routes with different passenger numbers and probabilities
images.description: Two side-by-side comparisons: Left side shows Route A with 600 passengers and 2% probability, showing calculation boxes leading to 12 expected refunds. Right side shows Route B with 400 passengers and 5% probability, leading to 20 expected refunds. Include a comparison bar showing Route A vs Route B outcomes.

fields.concept_tag: expected_outcome_comparison
fields.enabling_objective: Compare expected outcomes when given different probability and total number combinations

fields.teacher_script: Here's a real-world application. A restaurant in Victoria, Seychelles, serves 250 meals per day. Market research shows that 8% of customers will order dessert. If desserts sell for 150 SCR each, how much revenue does the restaurant expect from dessert sales on a typical day? Show all your working.
fields.question: A restaurant in Victoria, Seychelles, serves 250 meals per day. Market research shows that 8% of customers will order dessert. If desserts sell for 150 SCR each, how much revenue does the restaurant expect from dessert sales on a typical day?
fields.hint_1: First, find the expected number of desserts sold using 0.08 × 250.
fields.hint_2: Then multiply the expected number of desserts by the price per dessert (150 SCR).
fields.hint_3: Expected revenue = (expected desserts) × 150

images.caption: Real-world expected outcome problems often involve an additional multiplication step for revenue or cost.
images.alt_text: Restaurant scenario showing customer count, expected dessert orders, and revenue calculation
images.description: A restaurant setting showing: 250 customers represented as simple figures. Highlight 8% (approximately 20 figures) as ordering dessert. Show a dessert plate with the price label '150 SCR'. Include the calculation: 0.08 × 250 = 20 desserts, then 20 × 150 = 3000 SCR.

fields.concept_tag: expected_outcome_application
fields.enabling_objective: Apply the expected outcome formula to solve real-world scenario problems

fields.teacher_script: Let's check your understanding with a true or false question. Read the statement carefully and decide if it is correct or incorrect based on what we've learned.
fields.question: If a manufacturing company produces 8000 items per month and 0.5% of items are expected to be defective, then the expected number of defective items is 40 items per month.
fields.hint_1: Convert the percentage 0.5% to a decimal: 0.5 ÷ 100 = 0.005
fields.hint_2: Apply the formula: Expected Outcome = 0.005 × 8000
fields.hint_3: Perform the multiplication: 0.005 × 8000 = 40. Is the statement correct?

images.caption: The expected outcome of 40 defective items represents the average number we predict across many production months.
images.alt_text: Manufacturing production line showing 8000 items with 0.5% defective rate highlighted, equalling 40 defective items
images.description: A production line diagram showing 8000 items represented in rows. A small fraction (0.5%) are highlighted in red as defective, totalling 40 items. Include the calculation box: '0.5% = 0.005, Expected defective = 0.005 × 8000 = 40'. Label clearly.

fields.concept_tag: expected_outcome_mastery
fields.enabling_objective: Identify the total number of trials or occurrences from a given problem

fields.teacher_script: Corresponding angles are angles that are in the SAME position at each intersection point. When a transversal cuts two parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal. For example, look at the diagram — angle 1 is in the top-left position at the upper intersection, and angle 5 is in the top-left position at the lower intersection. These are corresponding angles, so angle 1 = angle 5. Think of it like matching bookmarks in two identical books: they're always in the same spot.
fields.concept_tag: corresponding_angles
fields.enabling_objective: Identify corresponding angles formed when a transversal crosses two parallel lines

fields.teacher_script: Let's work through a complete example. Look at the diagram — lines l and m are parallel, line t is the transversal, and angle 1 measures 65°. We need to find angle 5. Since angle 1 and angle 5 are corresponding angles, and the lines are parallel, they must be equal. Follow the working below:

images.caption: Corresponding angles are equal when lines are parallel.
images.alt_text: Parallel lines l and m cut by transversal t. Angle 1 = 65° at top; angle 5 = ? at bottom. Corresponding angles are colour-matched.
images.description: Two horizontal parallel lines labelled l and m, cut by a diagonal transversal t. At the top intersection, angle 1 is clearly labelled as 65°. At the bottom intersection, angle 5 is labelled with a question mark to show it is unknown. The corresponding angle pair (1 and 5) are highlighted in the same colour.

fields.concept_tag: corresponding_angles
fields.enabling_objective: Calculate the measure of an unknown angle using the property that corresponding angles are equal

fields.teacher_script: Now it's your turn. Use the diagram below to find the unknown angle.
fields.question: Lines l and m are parallel. Transversal t crosses both lines. Angle 2 = 48°. What is angle 6 (the corresponding angle)?
fields.hint_1: Are angles 2 and 6 in the same relative position at their respective intersections?
fields.hint_2: If two angles are corresponding angles formed by a transversal cutting parallel lines, what do we know about their measures?
fields.hint_3: Since angle 2 = 48°, and angle 6 is the corresponding angle, angle 6 must equal the same measure.

images.caption: Find angle 6 using the corresponding angles property.

images.description: Two horizontal parallel lines labelled l and m, cut by a diagonal transversal t. At the top intersection, angle 2 is labelled as 48°. At the bottom intersection, angle 6 is marked with a question mark. Angles 2 and 6 are highlighted in the same colour to indicate they are corresponding angles.

fields.concept_tag: corresponding_angles
fields.enabling_objective: Calculate the measure of an unknown angle using the property that corresponding angles are equal

fields.teacher_script: Alternate exterior angles are on opposite sides of the transversal and OUTSIDE (exterior to) the two parallel lines. Just like alternate interior angles, these are also equal when the lines are parallel. For example, angle 1 (above the upper line on the left) and angle 8 (below the lower line on the right) are alternate exterior angles. They're on opposite sides of the transversal and in the exterior regions.

images.caption: Alternate exterior angles are on opposite sides and in the exterior regions.
images.alt_text: Parallel lines with angles 1 and 8 highlighted as alternate exterior angles in shaded exterior regions.
images.description: Two horizontal parallel lines labelled l and m, with a diagonal transversal t crossing both. Eight angles numbered 1–8. Angles 1 and 8 are highlighted in the same colour — angle 1 is above line l on the left of the transversal; angle 8 is below line m on the right of the transversal. The exterior regions (above line l and below line m) are lightly shaded. A label indicates 'Exterior region' for both shaded areas.

fields.concept_tag: alternate_exterior_angles
fields.enabling_objective: Identify alternate exterior angles formed when a transversal crosses two parallel lines

fields.teacher_script: Use the diagram to answer this question about alternate interior angles.
fields.question: Lines l and m are parallel, cut by transversal t. Angle 3 = 72°. Find angle 6 (the alternate interior angle).
fields.hint_1: Are angles 3 and 6 on opposite sides of the transversal?
fields.hint_2: Are they both between the two parallel lines (interior)?
fields.hint_3: If they are alternate interior angles and the lines are parallel, what property tells us their measures?

images.caption: Find angle 6 using the alternate interior angles property.
images.alt_text: Parallel lines with angle 3 = 72° (top right interior) and angle 6 = ? (bottom left interior). Both are interior, opposite-side angles.
images.description: Two horizontal parallel lines labelled l and m, cut by a diagonal transversal t. At the top intersection, angle 3 is labelled 72°. At the bottom intersection, angle 6 is marked with a question mark. The interior region is shaded. Angles 3 and 6 are highlighted in the same colour and positioned on opposite sides of the transversal.

fields.concept_tag: alternate_interior_angles
fields.enabling_objective: Calculate the measure of an unknown angle using the property that alternate interior angles are equal

fields.teacher_script: Co-interior angles (also called same-side interior angles or consecutive interior angles) are on the SAME side of the transversal and both between the parallel lines. Unlike corresponding and alternate angles, co-interior angles are NOT equal — instead, they are supplementary (they add up to 180°). For example, angles 3 and 5 are both on the right side of the transversal and between the parallel lines, so angle 3 + angle 5 = 180°.

images.caption: Co-interior angles are supplementary (sum to 180°).
images.alt_text: Parallel lines with angles 3 and 5 highlighted as co-interior angles on the same side of the transversal.
images.description: Two horizontal parallel lines labelled l and m, with a diagonal transversal t crossing both. Eight angles numbered 1–8. Angles 3 and 5 are highlighted in the same colour — both are on the right side of the transversal and between the two parallel lines (interior). The interior region is lightly shaded. A label indicates '+' between the angles to show they sum to 180°.

fields.concept_tag: co_interior_angles
fields.enabling_objective: Identify co-interior (same-side interior) angles formed when a transversal crosses two parallel lines

fields.teacher_script: Now use the co-interior angle property to find the unknown angle.
fields.question: Lines l and m are parallel, cut by transversal t. Angle 4 = 110°. What is angle 8 (the co-interior angle on the same side)?
fields.hint_1: Are angles 4 and 8 on the same side of the transversal and both interior?
fields.hint_2: What property applies to co-interior angles when lines are parallel?
fields.hint_3: If angle 4 = 110°, and co-interior angles sum to 180°, then angle 8 = 180° − 110°.

images.caption: Find angle 8 using the co-interior angles property (sum = 180°).
images.alt_text: Parallel lines with angle 4 = 110° (top right interior) and angle 8 = ? (bottom right interior). Both are co-interior angles.
images.description: Two horizontal parallel lines labelled l and m, cut by a diagonal transversal t. At the top intersection, angle 4 is labelled 110°. At the bottom intersection, angle 8 is marked with a question mark. The interior region is shaded. Angles 4 and 8 are highlighted in the same colour, both on the right side of the transversal.

fields.concept_tag: co_interior_angles
fields.enabling_objective: Apply the property that co-interior angles are supplementary to solve for an unknown angle

fields.teacher_script: Today we're going to explore three different ways to describe how likely something is to happen. In Seychelles, weather forecasters use these three forms when they say 'There's a 70% chance of rain tomorrow' or 'The probability is 0.7'. By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to switch between all three forms and understand what they mean. Let's start with a real Seychelles example: imagine you're picking one island at random from the 115 islands in Seychelles. How do we describe the probability of picking Mahé specifically?

images.caption: The same probability can be written as a fraction, decimal, or percentage — they all mean the same thing.
images.alt_text: Three representations of probability for selecting Mahé from 115 Seychelles islands shown as fraction, decimal, and percentage
images.description: A map showing the Seychelles with three inset boxes displaying the same probability value in three different formats: (1) 1/115 as a fraction, (2) 0.0087 as a decimal, (3) 0.87% as a percentage. Each format has a label and colour-coding to show they represent the same probability.

fields.concept_tag: probability_representations

fields.teacher_script: A fraction has two parts: the numerator (top number) tells you how many outcomes you want, and the denominator (bottom number) tells you the total number of possible outcomes. When we write 3/5, the 3 is the numerator and the 5 is the denominator. For example, if you roll a standard die and want to find the probability of rolling a number less than 4, you have 3 favourable outcomes (1, 2, or 3) out of 6 possible outcomes, so the fraction is 3/6. The numerator is always smaller than or equal to the denominator, because you can't have more desired outcomes than total outcomes.

images.caption: The numerator is what we want; the denominator is all possibilities.
images.alt_text: Diagram showing numerator and denominator of fraction 3/5 with shaded boxes representing the fraction visually
images.description: A fraction bar diagram showing 3/5 with labels pointing to the 3 (numerator - 'desired outcomes') and 5 (denominator - 'total possible outcomes'). Below it, show a visual representation: 5 equal boxes in a row, with 3 boxes shaded to represent 3/5.

fields.concept_tag: probability_representations
fields.enabling_objective: Identify the numerator and denominator in a fraction representing probability

fields.teacher_script: Let's work through how to convert the fraction 4/5 into a decimal. This is a crucial skill because computers and calculators often use decimals. I'll show you every step, then we'll convert it to a percentage as well.

key_points: Numerator ÷ Denominator = Decimal form
Decimal × 100 = Percentage form
All three forms (fraction, decimal, percentage) represent the same probability value

steps.explanation: To convert a fraction to a decimal, divide the top number by the bottom number. We divide 4 ÷ 5.
4 ÷ 5 = 0.8. If you use long division: 4.0 ÷ 5 = 0.8 with no remainder.
Multiply the decimal by 100 and add a % sign: 0.8 × 100 = 80%.
4/5 = 0.8 = 80%. All three forms represent the same probability.

worked_example.problem: Convert the probability fraction 4/5 into decimal form, then into a percentage.

common_mistakes: Dividing denominator by numerator instead of numerator by denominator (e.g., 5 ÷ 4 = 1.25, which is wrong for probability)
Forgetting to multiply by 100 when converting from decimal to percentage
Writing 0.8% instead of 80% (forgetting that 0.8 is already the decimal form)

images.caption: Divide the numerator by the denominator: 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8.
images.alt_text: Step-by-step conversion of fraction 4/5 to decimal 0.8 using division, with number line showing position
images.description: Step-by-step conversion shown vertically: (Step 1) Start with 4/5. (Step 2) Show long division: 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8. (Step 3) Show a horizontal line with marks at 0, 0.4, 0.8, and 1.0, with 0.8 highlighted. Below the line, label '0 is impossible' and '1 is certain'. Add the annotation '0.8 is quite likely'.

fields.concept_tag: probability_representations
fields.enabling_objective: Convert a probability fraction to its equivalent decimal form

fields.teacher_script: Now let's practise converting fractions to decimals. Remember to divide the numerator by the denominator.
fields.question: Convert the fraction 3/4 to decimal form. Show your working: divide 3 by 4.
fields.hint_1: To convert a fraction to a decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator.
fields.hint_2: You need to divide 3 by 4. Try long division: 3.00 ÷ 4.
fields.hint_3: After dividing, you should get 0.75 (3 ÷ 4 = 0.75).

images.caption: Divide the numerator by the denominator to convert to decimal.
images.alt_text: Fraction 3/4 with division symbol and question mark for decimal answer
images.description: Show the fraction 3/4 with a large division symbol and the numerator and denominator labelled. Include an empty answer box with 'Decimal = ?' to be filled in.

fields.concept_tag: probability_representations
fields.enabling_objective: Convert a probability fraction to its equivalent decimal form

fields.teacher_script: In this example, we'll convert a decimal to a percentage. This is important for weather reports and news announcements.
fields.question: A weather forecast shows a 0.65 probability of rain in Victoria tomorrow. Convert this decimal to a percentage. Show your working.
fields.hint_1: To convert a decimal to a percentage, multiply by 100.
fields.hint_2: Take 0.65 and multiply it by 100: 0.65 × 100.
fields.hint_3: 0.65 × 100 = 65, so the answer is 65%.

images.caption: Multiply the decimal by 100 to get the percentage.
images.alt_text: Decimal 0.65 being converted to percentage on a scale from 0% to 100%
images.description: Show the decimal 0.65 with an arrow pointing to a multiplication symbol and 100. Below, show a partially filled percentage scale from 0% to 100% with 65% marked and 'Percentage = ?' for the student to complete.

fields.concept_tag: probability_representations
fields.enabling_objective: Convert a probability decimal to its equivalent percentage

fields.teacher_script: A common mistake students make is confusing the order of operations when converting. Many write 0.8% when they mean 80% — they forget to multiply by 100. Another mistake is dividing denominator by numerator instead of numerator by denominator. Remember: the numerator (what you want) always goes first in the division. For the fraction 1/5, you divide 1 by 5, not 5 by 1. Finally, some students think that 0.5 and 50% are different — they're not! They represent exactly the same probability.

images.caption: Avoid these three common mistakes: forgetting to multiply by 100, reversing the division, and thinking equivalent forms are different.
images.alt_text: Three common mistakes in probability conversion marked with X symbols and corrections with checkmarks
images.description: A comparison chart showing three common mistakes: (1) Writing 0.8% instead of 80% with a red X, (2) Dividing 5÷1 instead of 1÷5 with a red X, (3) Thinking 0.5 and 50% are different with a red X and green checkmark showing they're equal. Include the correct conversions below each.

fields.concept_tag: probability_representations

fields.teacher_script: Let's apply all three conversion skills to a real-world Seychelles example. You need to convert between fraction, decimal, and percentage forms.
fields.question: A shop in Victoria sells 2 red mangoes out of 5 total mangoes. What is the probability of picking a red mango as a fraction, decimal, and percentage?
fields.hint_1: Start by writing the fraction using the number of red mangoes (numerator) and total mangoes (denominator): 2/5.
fields.hint_2: Convert the fraction to a decimal by dividing 2 ÷ 5 = 0.4.
fields.hint_3: Convert the decimal to a percentage by multiplying by 100: 0.4 × 100 = 40%.

images.caption: Use the number of red mangoes and total mangoes to write all three forms of probability.
images.alt_text: Shop scenario showing 2 red mangoes out of 5 total with conversion boxes for fraction, decimal, and percentage
images.description: A shop shelf or basket showing 5 mangoes: 2 coloured red, 3 coloured yellow or orange. Label the image with 'Red mangoes = 2' and 'Total mangoes = 5'. Below, show three empty boxes labelled 'Fraction = ?', 'Decimal = ?', 'Percentage = ?'.

fields.concept_tag: probability_representations
fields.enabling_objective: Convert between all three representations of the same probability value

fields.teacher_script: When you compare probabilities in different forms, convert them to the same form first. Let's practice comparing a fraction and a decimal.
fields.question: Which probability is greater: 7/10 or 0.65?
choices: B) 0.65 is greater because decimals are always larger than fractions
D) They are equal because 7/10 and 0.65 both equal 75%
fields.hint_1: Convert both probabilities to the same form (decimal or percentage) to compare them.
fields.hint_2: Convert 7/10 to decimal form: 7 ÷ 10 = 0.7. Now compare 0.7 with 0.65.
fields.hint_3: Since 0.7 is greater than 0.65, the fraction 7/10 represents a greater probability.

images.caption: Place both probabilities on a number line to see which is greater.
images.alt_text: Number line showing 0.65 and 0.7 (7/10) to compare probabilities visually
images.description: A number line from 0 to 1 with markings at 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.65, 0.75, and 1. Show a marker for 0.65 and another for 0.7 (labelled as 7/10). Use colour or arrows to clearly show which value is further right.

fields.concept_tag: probability_representations
fields.enabling_objective: Compare two probability values given in different forms (fraction, decimal, or percentage)

fields.teacher_script: Different situations call for different forms of probability. Let's think about when percentages are most useful.
fields.question: A ferry ticket is drawn randomly from a box containing 500 tickets for travel between islands. Which representation would be MOST useful for a news announcement about winning: fraction (1/500), decimal (0.002), or percentage (0.2%)?
choices: A) Fraction, because it shows the exact numbers (1/500)
B) Percentage, because people understand percentages better than fractions or decimals
C) Decimal, because it is the most accurate (0.002)
D) All three are equally useful for news announcements
fields.hint_1: Think about who reads a news announcement — the general public, not just mathematicians.
fields.hint_2: Which form do you see most often in news reports about weather, sports, or surveys?
fields.hint_3: Percentages are used in news because they are familiar to everyday people.

images.caption: Percentages are most commonly used in news because they are familiar to the general public.
images.alt_text: News announcement comparing three probability representations for clarity
images.description: A mock newspaper headline or news broadcast screenshot showing the same probability in three formats side by side: '1/500 chance of winning ferry ticket' vs. '0.002 chance of winning ferry ticket' vs. '0.2% chance of winning ferry ticket'. Highlight or frame the percentage version as the most readable.

fields.concept_tag: probability_representations

fields.teacher_script: Now let's check your understanding with a final quiz question about identifying equivalent probability forms.
fields.question: A dice is rolled. The probability of rolling an even number (2, 4, or 6) is 3/6. This is equivalent to 0.5 and 50%.
fields.hint_1: Count the favourable outcomes: rolling a 2, 4, or 6 — that is 3 outcomes.
fields.hint_2: Count the total possible outcomes when rolling a standard dice: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 — that is 6 outcomes.
fields.hint_3: The probability is 3/6 = 0.5 = 50%, so the statement is true.

images.caption: 3 out of 6 faces on a dice are even: 3/6 = 0.5 = 50%.
images.alt_text: Dice showing 3 even-numbered faces out of 6 total faces with all three probability representations labelled
images.description: A standard 6-sided dice (cube) with faces numbered 1 to 6 visible. Show the even-numbered faces (2, 4, 6) highlighted or shaded in one colour, and odd-numbered faces (1, 3, 5) in another colour. Below, write '3 out of 6 faces are even' and show the fraction 3/6, decimal 0.5, and percentage 50% side by side.

fields.concept_tag: probability_representations

fields.teacher_script: Today we're learning one of the most powerful rules in probability — a rule that will help you solve many real-world problems. Look at the weather forecast for Seychelles: if the probability of rain tomorrow is 0.7, what's the probability it won't rain? This rule helps answer that question instantly.

images.caption: Complementary events span the entire probability scale from 0 to 1.
images.alt_text: A probability scale showing complementary events: P(rain) = 0.7 and P(no rain) = 0.3 summing to 1
images.description: A probability scale from 0 to 1 marked with fractions and decimals. Show a vertical line at 0.7 labeled 'P(rain) = 0.7' and another at 0.3 labeled 'P(no rain) = 0.3'. Above the scale, show two complementary events in boxes: 'It rains tomorrow' and 'It doesn't rain tomorrow'. Use an arrow to show they span the entire scale.

fields.concept_tag: complementary_probability

fields.teacher_script: The rule is simple: every event either happens or it doesn't happen. There's no third option. So the probability of an event happening plus the probability of it not happening must equal 1 (or 100%). We write this as: P(event) + P(not event) = 1. This means if you know one probability, you can always find the other by subtraction.

key_points: Every outcome either happens or doesn't happen — no third option.
Complementary events cover all possibilities; nothing is left out.
P(event) + P(not event) = 1 is always true.
This rule saves time: find one probability, subtract from 1 to get the other.

key_vocabulary.example: Event: 'Drawing a red card from a deck'. Complement: 'Drawing a black card'.
key_vocabulary.definition: The complement of an event is everything that is NOT that event. If the event is 'rolling a 6', the complement is 'rolling a 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5'.

key_vocabulary.example: P(heads) = 0.5 and P(tails) = 0.5 are complementary because 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.
key_vocabulary.definition: Two probabilities are complementary if their sum equals 1. They represent all possible outcomes.

educational_content.seychelles_context: Seychelles weather forecasts often state the probability of rain. If the forecast says there's a 0.6 probability of rain, the probability of no rain is 0.4. This rule helps fishermen and farmers plan their days.

images.caption: All possible outcomes divide into exactly two groups: the event and its complement.
images.alt_text: Flowchart showing outcome space dividing into an event and its complement
images.description: A flowchart showing the logic of complementary events. On the left: 'Outcome Space (All Possibilities)'. Two arrows point right to two circles: one labeled 'Event happens' with P(E), the other 'Event doesn't happen' with P(not E). Below both circles: 'P(E) + P(not E) = 1'.

fields.concept_tag: complementary_probability
fields.enabling_objective: Identify the complement of an event in a practical situation

fields.teacher_script: Let's work through a problem step by step. A fisherman in Seychelles has a 0.75 probability of catching fish on any given day. What's the probability he won't catch fish? Watch how I use the rule to find the answer.

steps.action: Identify the event and its complement
steps.explanation: Event: 'Catches fish'. Complement: 'Doesn't catch fish'. We are given P(catches fish) = 0.75, and we need to find P(doesn't catch fish).
We know that P(event) + P(not event) = 1. Substituting our event: P(catches fish) + P(doesn't catch fish) = 1.
We know P(catches fish) = 0.75, so: 0.75 + P(doesn't catch fish) = 1.
Subtract 0.75 from both sides: P(doesn't catch fish) = 1 − 0.75 = 0.25.
Check: 0.75 + 0.25 = 1.00 ✓. The probabilities sum to 1, so the answer is correct.

worked_example.problem: A fisherman has a probability of 0.75 of catching fish on any given day. What is the probability that he will NOT catch fish?

images.caption: The two complementary probabilities partition the entire probability scale.
images.alt_text: Probability bar showing P(catches fish) = 0.75 and P(doesn't catch fish) = 0.25 with total = 1
images.description: A horizontal bar showing the probability scale from 0 to 1. The bar is divided into two sections: the left section (0 to 0.75) is shaded blue and labeled 'P(catches fish) = 0.75'. The right section (0.75 to 1) is shaded orange and labeled 'P(doesn't catch fish) = 0.25'. Label the total length as 1.

fields.concept_tag: complementary_probability
fields.enabling_objective: Calculate the probability of an event not happening given the probability it will happen

fields.teacher_script: Now try this problem. A shop in Victoria tracks customer purchases. Use the complementary probability rule to find the answer.
fields.question: A shop in Victoria has a probability of 0.8 that a customer will buy something. What is the probability that a customer will NOT buy something?
fields.hint_1: Think about what must be true: P(event) + P(not event) must equal what?
fields.hint_2: You know P(buys something) = 0.8. Use the rule P(event) + P(not event) = 1 to set up an equation.
fields.hint_3: Substitute: 0.8 + P(doesn't buy) = 1. Now solve by subtracting 0.8 from both sides.
fields.concept_tag: complementary_probability
fields.enabling_objective: Calculate the probability of an event not happening given the probability it will happen

fields.teacher_script: Here's a second practice problem with a different scenario. Apply the rule to find the probability of the complement.
fields.question: The probability that a visitor to Seychelles will visit the Anse Source d'Argent beach is 0.35. What is the probability that a visitor will NOT visit this beach?
fields.hint_1: Start by identifying the two complementary events: visiting and not visiting the beach.
fields.hint_2: Write the rule: P(visits) + P(doesn't visit) = 1. Substitute P(visits) = 0.35.
fields.hint_3: Solve: 0.35 + P(doesn't visit) = 1, so P(doesn't visit) = 1 − 0.35.
fields.concept_tag: complementary_probability
fields.enabling_objective: Apply the complementary probability rule to solve for an unknown probability

fields.teacher_script: A very common mistake is forgetting that probabilities must sum to 1. Some students see 0.35 and think the complement is simply 0.65, but then forget to CHECK that 0.35 + 0.65 = 1. Always verify by adding — if they don't sum to 1, you've made an error. Another mistake: students sometimes confuse the event with its complement and calculate the wrong one. Read carefully: if the question asks for 'probability of not raining', don't give 'probability of raining'.

common_mistakes: Forgetting to check that the probabilities sum to 1. Always verify: P(event) + P(not event) should equal exactly 1.
Confusing which event is which. If asked for P(not raining), don't give P(raining). Underline the key words in the question.
Using decimal and percentage interchangeably without converting. If given 35%, convert to 0.35 before calculating, or work entirely in percentages.

images.caption: Always verify: complementary probabilities must sum exactly to 1.
images.alt_text: Comparison showing an incorrect complementary probability (no verification) versus correct calculation (verified to sum to 1)
images.description: Two side-by-side probability scales. Left scale (WRONG): shows a section at 0.35 labeled 'P(event) = 0.35' and another section labeled 'P(not event) = ?' with a red X. Right scale (CORRECT): shows 0.35 for P(event) and 0.65 for P(not event), with a green checkmark and '0.35 + 0.65 = 1'.

fields.concept_tag: complementary_probability
fields.enabling_objective: Verify that probabilities of an event and its complement sum to 1

fields.teacher_script: Now you'll solve and verify. Apply the rule AND check that your probabilities sum to 1.
fields.question: A weather service reports that the probability of cyclone warnings in Seychelles during a given month is 0.12. (a) What is the probability of NO cyclone warnings? (b) Verify that the two probabilities sum to 1.
fields.hint_1: First, find P(no warnings) using P(event) + P(not event) = 1.
fields.hint_2: Substitute: 0.12 + P(no warnings) = 1. Solve for P(no warnings).
fields.hint_3: Then check your work: add 0.12 + 0.88. Do they equal 1? If yes, you're correct.
fields.concept_tag: complementary_probability
fields.enabling_objective: Verify that probabilities of an event and its complement sum to 1

fields.teacher_script: Here's a real-world application. Use the complementary probability rule first, then multiply by the sample size to find the expected number.
fields.question: A tourism agency surveys visitors to Seychelles. The probability that a visitor will stay more than 7 days is 0.55. If 200 visitors are surveyed, how many are expected to stay 7 days or fewer?
fields.hint_1: Start by finding P(stay 7 days or fewer) using the complement of P(stay more than 7 days).
fields.hint_2: P(more than 7 days) = 0.55, so P(7 days or fewer) = 1 − 0.55 = 0.45.
fields.hint_3: Now multiply: number of visitors expected = 0.45 × 200. Show your working.
fields.concept_tag: complementary_probability
fields.enabling_objective: Solve practical problems using the fact that P(event) + P(not event) = 1

fields.teacher_script: Evaluate whether this statement about attendance and absence is correct by checking the rule.
fields.question: True or False: If P(a student attends school on a random day) = 0.92, then P(student is absent) = 0.08.
fields.hint_1: Identify the event and its complement: attending school and being absent. These should be complementary.
fields.hint_2: Use the rule: P(attends) + P(absent) = 1. Substitute: 0.92 + P(absent) = 1.
fields.hint_3: Solve: P(absent) = 1 − 0.92 = 0.08. Does this match the statement?
fields.concept_tag: complementary_probability
fields.enabling_objective: Convert between complementary probability statements and equations

fields.teacher_script: Now test your understanding. Use the complementary probability rule to find the probability of an unsuccessful catch and select the correct answer.
fields.question: A fishing boat captain estimates that the probability of a successful catch on any outing is 0.68. What is the probability of an unsuccessful catch?
fields.hint_1: You need to find P(unsuccessful), which is the complement of P(successful) = 0.68.
fields.hint_2: Use the rule: P(successful) + P(unsuccessful) = 1.
fields.hint_3: Substitute and solve: 0.68 + P(unsuccessful) = 1, so P(unsuccessful) = 1 − 0.68 = 0.32.

key_points: The complementary probability rule P(event) + P(not event) = 1 applies to every scenario.
Always verify by adding the two probabilities — they must sum to exactly 1.
This rule is a shortcut: if you know one probability, you instantly know the other.

fields.concept_tag: complementary_probability

fields.teacher_script: Probability measures how likely something is to happen. We calculate it as a fraction: the number of ways something CAN happen (favorable outcomes) divided by the total number of possible outcomes. The formula is: Probability = Favorable Outcomes ÷ Total Possible Outcomes. For the raffle: you could win (favorable) or lose (not favorable). There are 5 ways to win out of 20 possible draws, so the probability is 5/20.

images.caption: Probability formula: divide favorable outcomes by all possible outcomes.
images.alt_text: The probability formula with the raffle example worked out.
images.description: A box labelled 'Probability Formula' containing the equation: Probability = Favorable Outcomes ÷ Total Possible Outcomes. Below it, show the raffle example: Favorable Outcomes = 5 (winning tickets), Total Possible Outcomes = 20 (all tickets), Probability = 5/20. Use clear, large text.

fields.concept_tag: probability_ratio
fields.enabling_objective: Identify the total number of possible outcomes in a simple event

fields.teacher_script: Once you have your probability fraction, you can convert it to a decimal by dividing the numerator by the denominator. A probability is always between 0 and 1: a probability of 0 means something will never happen, and a probability of 1 means it will definitely happen. For example, 1/4 = 0.25, which means a 25% chance. Let's convert some common fractions: 1/2 = 0.5, 1/5 = 0.2, 3/4 = 0.75.

key_points: Divide the numerator by the denominator to convert fraction to decimal.
Probability ranges from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).
Multiplying the decimal by 100 gives the percentage.

fields.concept_tag: probability_decimal
fields.enabling_objective: Convert a probability ratio to a decimal between 0 and 1

fields.teacher_script: Try this slightly harder problem. Count both the favorable outcomes and total outcomes, then simplify your fraction.
fields.question: A spinner has 12 equal sections: 4 sections are yellow, 5 sections are green, and 3 sections are red. If you spin once, what is the probability the spinner lands on yellow?
fields.hint_1: Count all the sections on the spinner—this is your total possible outcomes.
fields.hint_2: How many sections are yellow? (This is your favorable outcomes.)
fields.hint_3: Write the fraction Favorable ÷ Total, then simplify by finding the greatest common factor.

images.caption: Spinner with 12 equal sections in three colours.
images.alt_text: A spinner with 12 sections: 4 yellow, 5 green, and 3 red.
images.description: A circular spinner divided into 12 equal sections. Colour 4 sections yellow, 5 sections green, and 3 sections red. Add a pointer in the center. Label the counts: '4 yellow, 5 green, 3 red, 12 total'.

fields.concept_tag: probability_ratio
fields.enabling_objective: Identify the number of favorable outcomes for a given event

fields.teacher_script: Convert this fraction to a decimal by dividing the top by the bottom.
fields.question: Convert the probability 3/12 to a decimal. Show your working.
fields.hint_1: First simplify the fraction 3/12.
fields.hint_2: Then divide the numerator by the denominator.
fields.hint_3: Check: 1 ÷ 4 should give you a decimal.
fields.concept_tag: probability_decimal
fields.enabling_objective: Convert a probability ratio to a decimal between 0 and 1

fields.teacher_script: Calculate the probability for each event, then compare them to decide which is more likely.
fields.question: Two friends are playing games. Event A: rolling a 6 on a standard die (1 die, 6 sides, one side shows 6). Event B: picking a red card from a standard deck (52 cards, 26 red). Which event is more likely? Show the probability for each event and explain your answer.
fields.expected_answer: Event A: 1/6 ≈ 0.167. Event B: 26/52 = 1/2 = 0.5. Event B is more likely because 0.5 > 0.167.
fields.hint_1: For Event A: 1 side has a 6 out of 6 sides total.
fields.hint_2: For Event B: 26 red cards out of 52 total cards.
fields.hint_3: Compare the decimals or simplified fractions to decide which is more likely.
fields.concept_tag: probability_comparison
fields.enabling_objective: Compare the likelihood of two events using their calculated probabilities

fields.teacher_script: Now show me you can calculate a single-event probability from scratch using the formula you learned.
fields.question: A box contains 6 green pencils, 4 blue pencils, and 2 red pencils. You pick one pencil without looking. What is the probability that it is blue?
fields.hint_1: Count the total number of pencils in the box.
fields.hint_2: Count how many pencils are blue.
fields.hint_3: Write Favorable Outcomes ÷ Total Possible Outcomes.

images.caption: Find the probability of picking a blue pencil.
images.alt_text: A box containing 6 green pencils, 4 blue pencils, and 2 red pencils.
images.description: A box showing 12 pencils: 6 green, 4 blue, and 2 red. Each group is clearly separated and labelled with its count and colour. The question mark sits above the box indicating 'pick one pencil'.

fields.teacher_script: This is your final quiz question. A straight line is divided by two rays into three angles: 30°, 62°, and w. What is the value of w?
fields.question: A straight line is divided by two rays into three angles: 30°, 62°, and w. What is the value of w?
fields.hint_1: All three angles on a straight line must sum to 180°.
fields.hint_2: Write the equation: 30° + 62° + w = 180°

images.caption: Find the missing angle w on this straight line.
images.alt_text: Straight line divided by two rays into three angles: 30°, 62°, and w
images.description: A horizontal straight line with two rays extending upward from a point on the line, dividing it into three angles. Label the angles as '30°', '62°', and 'w = ?'. Mark the straight line with arrows at both ends.

fields.concept_tag: straight_line_angles

fields.teacher_script: Next, extract the relationship from the diagram into an equation. Look at the diagram: we have one bag of x mangoes, plus another bag of x mangoes, plus 3 loose mangoes, and this equals 15 in total. In algebra, we write this as: x + x + 3 = 15. Notice: addition is shown by side-by-side items; the total is shown after the equals sign.

images.caption: Every part of the diagram translates into a part of the equation.
images.alt_text: Two-column diagram showing visual representation converting to algebraic equation
images.description: Side-by-side comparison: on the left, the market-stall diagram (two bags + 3 loose = 15 total); on the right, the matching equation 'x + x + 3 = 15' with an arrow pointing from each diagram element to its algebraic equivalent.

fields.concept_tag: solving_diagram_equations
fields.enabling_objective: Extract numerical values and relationships from a labeled diagram

fields.teacher_script: Now you'll solve a similar problem with different numbers. Write the equation from the diagram, then solve step by step, showing your work.
fields.question: Look at the diagram below showing three identical boxes of coconuts plus 5 loose coconuts, totalling 20 coconuts. Write the equation and solve for the number of coconuts in each box.
fields.expected_answer: Equation: x + x + x + 5 = 20 or 3x + 5 = 20. Solution: subtract 5 from both sides: 3x = 15. Divide both sides by 3: x = 5. Each box contains 5 coconuts.
fields.hint_1: Start by writing what you see in the diagram as an equation. How many identical boxes are there? That tells you how many x's you have.
fields.hint_2: Once you have the equation, your first step is to subtract 5 from both sides. What do you get?
fields.hint_3: After subtracting, you'll have 3x = 15. Now divide both sides by 3.

images.caption: Identify the unknown (x), count how many boxes, and write the equation.
images.alt_text: Three identical boxes plus 5 loose coconuts totalling 20 coconuts
images.description: Market diagram showing three identical boxes labelled 'x coconuts' each, plus 5 loose coconuts, equalling 20 total coconuts. Each element clearly labelled and positioned.

fields.concept_tag: solving_diagram_equations

fields.teacher_script: Apply your skills to this real-world Seychelles context problem. Set up the equation, solve, and show your verification.
fields.question: A boat travelling between two Seychelles islands covers a distance in three equal legs. If each leg is x km and the total distance is 48 km, write and solve the equation. Then state how far the boat travels in each leg.
fields.expected_answer: Equation: x + x + x = 48 or 3x = 48. Divide both sides by 3: x = 16 km. The boat travels 16 km in each leg.
fields.hint_1: Three equal legs means you have three x's to add together.
fields.hint_2: Write: x + x + x = 48, which simplifies to 3x = 48.
fields.hint_3: To isolate x, divide both sides by 3. What is 48 ÷ 3?

images.caption: Three equal legs of x km each sum to a total of 48 km.
images.alt_text: Three islands connected by three equal distance segments totalling 48 km
images.description: Schematic map of three Seychelles islands connected by three line segments labelled 'x km' each, with a total distance label of 48 km. Simplified, not to scale.

fields.concept_tag: solving_diagram_equations
fields.enabling_objective: Apply the solution to answer a question about the diagram's measurements or properties

fields.teacher_script: Solve this triangle problem and make sure to verify by checking that your answer satisfies the original equation.
fields.question: A diagram shows two sides of a triangle: one side is x, the other is 8 units, and the third is twice the first side. If the perimeter is 32 units, solve for x and then verify your answer by checking that all three sides add up to 32.
fields.expected_answer: Equation: x + 8 + 2x = 32. Simplify: 3x + 8 = 32. Subtract 8: 3x = 24. Divide by 3: x = 8. Verify: 8 + 8 + 2(8) = 8 + 8 + 16 = 32 ✓
fields.hint_1: Identify all three sides: one is x, one is 8, and one is 2x (twice the first).
fields.hint_2: Write the perimeter equation: x + 8 + 2x = 32. Combine the x terms first: 3x + 8 = 32.
fields.hint_3: Subtract 8 from both sides, then divide by 3 to find x. Check your answer by adding all three sides.

images.caption: Three sides, one of which is twice another, form a perimeter of 32 units.
images.alt_text: Triangle with sides x, 8, and 2x, perimeter 32
images.description: Triangle with three sides labelled: 'x', '8', and '2x'. The perimeter = 32 is stated below. No values are yet solved; this shows the setup only.

fields.concept_tag: solving_diagram_equations
fields.enabling_objective: Substitute a calculated value back into the original diagram to verify the solution

fields.teacher_script: Solve this angle problem. Remember that supplementary angles on a straight line always add to 180 degrees.
fields.question: Two angles in a diagram are supplementary (they add up to 180°). One angle is (3x + 20)° and the other is x°. Write and solve the equation to find the value of x, then calculate both angles.
fields.expected_answer: Equation: (3x + 20) + x = 180. Simplify: 4x + 20 = 180. Subtract 20: 4x = 160. Divide by 4: x = 40. First angle: 40°. Second angle: 3(40) + 20 = 120 + 20 = 140°. Verify: 40 + 140 = 180 ✓
fields.hint_1: Supplementary angles add to 180°, so write: (3x + 20) + x = 180.
fields.hint_2: Combine like terms: 3x + x = 4x, so you have 4x + 20 = 180.
fields.hint_3: Subtract 20 from both sides to get 4x = 160, then divide by 4 to find x = 40.

images.caption: Supplementary angles on a straight line add up to 180°.
images.alt_text: Two supplementary angles labelled (3x + 20)° and x° on a straight line
images.description: Two adjacent angles on a straight line, labelled (3x + 20)° and x°, forming a straight angle of 180°. The angle arcs are clearly shown.

fields.concept_tag: solving_diagram_equations
fields.enabling_objective: Interpret and use geometric diagrams (angles, lengths, areas) to set up equations

fields.teacher_script: Now it's your turn. A fishing company in Seychelles has 200 fishing nets. Experience shows that 12% of nets will get damaged by storms in any given season. How many nets do you expect to be damaged this season? Show your working step-by-step.
fields.question: A fishing company in Seychelles has 200 fishing nets. Experience shows that 12% of nets will get damaged by storms in any given season. How many nets do you expect to be damaged this season?
fields.hint_1: Start by converting the percentage 12% into a decimal (divide by 100).
fields.hint_2: Once you have the decimal probability, multiply it by the total number of nets (200).
fields.hint_3: The calculation is: 0.12 × 200. What do you get?

images.caption: Expected outcome shows which nets, on average, will experience the event.
images.alt_text: Grid of 200 fishing nets with approximately 24 highlighted in red to show expected damage
images.description: A schematic showing 200 fishing nets arranged in a grid. Highlight approximately 24 of them in red (damaged) and leave the rest in blue. Include a label: 'Total nets = 200, Probability of damage = 12% = 0.12, Expected damaged = ?'

fields.concept_tag: expected_outcome_concept
fields.enabling_objective: Calculate expected outcome by multiplying probability by total number

fields.teacher_script: Here's a slightly different problem. A school in Seychelles has 450 students. A new vaccination programme expects to prevent disease in 96% of vaccinated students. How many students in the school do we expect to be protected?
fields.question: A school in Seychelles has 450 students. A new vaccination programme expects to prevent disease in 96% of vaccinated students. How many students in the school do we expect to be protected?
fields.hint_1: Remember: 96% means 96 out of every 100, which is 0.96 as a decimal.
fields.hint_2: Multiply the probability (as a decimal) by the total number of students.
fields.hint_3: 0.96 × 450 = ? (Hint: Think of it as 450 − 4% of 450)

images.caption: Expected outcome calculations often result in splitting a total into proportional groups.
images.alt_text: Bar chart comparing protected (432) vs unprotected (18) students out of 450
images.description: A bar chart with two bars: left bar shows 'Protected students (96%)' reaching 432 on a scale of 0–450, right bar shows 'Unprotected students (4%)' reaching 18. Label the scale, percentages, and final numbers clearly.

fields.concept_tag: expected_outcome_concept
fields.enabling_objective: Calculate expected outcome by multiplying probability by total number

fields.teacher_script: A common mistake students make is to forget to convert percentages to decimals before multiplying. For example, some students write: Expected Outcome = 12 × 200 = 2400, using the percentage number directly instead of the decimal. This is wrong — you must convert 12% to 0.12 first. Another mistake is to forget to interpret the answer in context. If the answer is 18, you should say '18 boats' or '18 nets', not just '18'. Always check: Does my answer make sense in the real-world situation?

images.caption: Convert percentages to decimals before multiplying in the expected outcome formula.
images.alt_text: Side-by-side comparison of incorrect percentage multiplication vs correct decimal conversion
images.description: A comparison diagram showing 'Common Mistake' on the left side: '12% × 200 = 12 × 200 = 2400 ✗ WRONG' with an red X. On the right side, 'Correct Method': '12% = 0.12, then 0.12 × 200 = 24 ✓ CORRECT' with a green checkmark. Include a note: 'Always convert percentages to decimals first!'

fields.concept_tag: expected_outcome_mistakes
fields.enabling_objective: Interpret the calculated expected outcome in context of the problem

fields.teacher_script: Now let's try a multi-step problem. A coconut plantation in Seychelles has 5000 coconut trees. Each year, 3% of trees are expected to be damaged by disease. The plantation owner wants to know how many trees to plant as replacements. They also decide to plant 50 extra trees for future growth. How many trees should they plant in total?
fields.question: A coconut plantation in Seychelles has 5000 coconut trees. Each year, 3% of trees are expected to be damaged by disease. The owner plans to plant replacement trees for the damaged ones, plus 50 extra trees for future growth. How many trees should the owner plant in total?
fields.hint_1: First, calculate the expected number of damaged trees using the expected outcome formula (0.03 × 5000).
fields.hint_2: Then add the 50 extra trees for growth to the number of replacement trees.
fields.hint_3: Total trees to plant = damaged trees + 50

fields.teacher_script: Now I'll solve the mango-bag equation step by step, showing every line of working so you can see exactly how we find the value of x.

key_points: Simplify like terms first (x + x = 2x)
Use inverse operations (subtract, then divide) to isolate x
Always do the same operation to both sides of the equation

steps.action: Write the equation from the diagram
steps.explanation: From the diagram: x + x + 3 = 15

steps.action: Simplify the left side by combining like terms
steps.explanation: x + x = 2x, so the equation becomes: 2x + 3 = 15

steps.action: Subtract 3 from both sides to isolate the term with x
steps.explanation: 2x + 3 − 3 = 15 − 3, which gives us: 2x = 12

steps.action: Divide both sides by 2 to find x
Check: substitute x = 6 back into the original equation

worked_example.problem: Two identical bags of mangoes plus 3 loose mangoes total 15 mangoes. Write and solve the equation to find how many mangoes are in each bag.

images.description: Annotated step-by-step solution showing the equation x + x + 3 = 15 transforming into 2x + 3 = 15, then 2x = 12, then x = 6. Each step is colour-coded and numbered. Include a check step showing 6 + 6 + 3 = 15.

fields.teacher_script: Imagine you're at the Friday night market in Victoria, and a stall is running a prize draw. There are 20 raffle tickets in a jar—5 of them win a free mango. If you buy one ticket, what's the chance you'll win? This is a probability question, and today we'll learn exactly how to answer it by counting outcomes and comparing them as a ratio.

images.caption: The prize draw: 5 winning tickets out of 20 total.
images.alt_text: A jar with 20 raffle tickets: 5 green (winning) and 15 white (non-winning).
images.description: A transparent jar containing 20 raffle tickets: 5 tickets coloured green (winning tickets) and 15 tickets coloured white (non-winning), with a hand reaching toward the jar. Label the jar 'Prize Draw' and add text '20 total tickets, 5 winning'.

fields.teacher_script: Let's work through the raffle problem step by step. We'll identify the outcomes and calculate the probability.

steps.explanation: Favorable outcomes are the results you want. Here, drawing a winning ticket is favorable. There are 5 winning tickets.
Total possible outcomes are all the results that could happen. Any of the 20 tickets could be drawn, so there are 20 total possible outcomes.

steps.action: Write the probability as a fraction
steps.explanation: Probability = Favorable Outcomes ÷ Total Possible Outcomes = 5 ÷ 20 = 5/20.
Divide both numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor. 5/20 = 1/4 (both divided by 5).

worked_example.problem: A raffle jar contains 20 tickets. 5 of them win a prize. What is the probability of drawing a winning ticket?

images.caption: Worked example: probability of winning the raffle is 1/4.

fields.teacher_script: Let's work through a real example from Seychelles highlands. A granite boulder sits on a mountainside. Water fills a crack in the rock. At night, the temperature drops to freezing, and the water expands as it freezes — this pressure pushes the crack wider. After many freeze-thaw cycles, the boulder eventually splits. We call this freeze-thaw weathering. This is just one cause of physical weathering. Other processes include exfoliation, where layers of rock peel away as pressure is released, and abrasion, where rocks are worn smooth by friction and impact. Now think about the rocks and mountains around you — which of these physical weathering processes do you think might be happening there right now?

fields.teacher_script: Weathering happens when rock breaks down over time through different processes. Physical weathering cracks rock through freeze-thaw cycles, where water freezes and expands in cracks, or through abrasion, where wind and water grind rock surfaces. Chemical weathering dissolves rock when rainwater and oxygen react with minerals, similar to how rust forms on metal. Biological weathering occurs when plants and animals break down rock—for example, tree roots growing into cracks can split rock apart, and lichens can chemically break down rock surfaces. All three types of weathering work together to reshape landscapes around us. Think about a rocky cliff or a stone wall near your home — which type of weathering do you think is affecting it most, and what evidence might you look for?

fields.teacher_script: Imagine you're standing at the top of a mountain on Mahe, and you spin slowly in a circle watching the ocean and islands. When you complete one full turn, you've rotated through all the angles around your position — that complete turn is always 360 degrees. Today we're learning why angles around a single point always add up to exactly 360 degrees, and how to use this to solve geometry problems.

fields.teacher_script: Look at any point. Around that point, you can draw multiple rays (straight lines starting from the point). The angles between these rays are called 'angles around a point'. No matter how many angles you create around a point, they must fit together perfectly to complete one full 360-degree rotation. Think of a pizza cut into slices: no matter how many slices you cut, the pieces all fit together to make one complete circle.

fields.question: A rectangular garden in Seychelles has a length that is twice its width. If the perimeter is 36 metres, find the width. (Perimeter = 2 × length + 2 × width. Let w = width.)

fields.teacher_script: A common mistake is forgetting to do the same operation to both sides of the equation. For example, if you have 2x + 3 = 15 and you subtract 3 from the left side only, you'll get 2x = 15, which is wrong. You must subtract 3 from both sides to keep the equation balanced—like a seesaw that stays level. Always remember: whatever you do to one side, do to the other.

key_points: Both sides of an equation must stay equal—like a balanced scale
Always perform the same operation on both sides
Combine like terms before isolating the variable
common_mistakes: Subtracting from only one side: 2x + 3 = 15 → 2x = 15 (wrong; should be 2x = 12)
Not combining like terms first: 2x + 3x + 5 = 30 → trying to solve without first adding 2x + 3x = 5x
Dividing only the variable: 2x = 12 → x = 12/2 gives 6, but if you write 'x = 12' you've forgotten to divide the right side

fields.teacher_script: Let's work through a real scenario. A rock on Morne Blanc has visible cracks that radiate outward, smaller pieces have broken off, and the interior of the broken pieces is still pale grey granite. Is this physical or chemical weathering? Let's think step by step: First, ask — did the rock's colour change? No, it's still pale grey inside. Second — did the mineral identity change? No, it's still the same granite. Third — what caused the damage? Daily temperature swings from sun-heated rock cooling at night. This is freeze-thaw action, which is mechanical, not chemical. So this is physical weathering. The key clue: the rock broke but stayed the same rock. Now, can you think of another example of physical weathering that might happen in your own area or somewhere you know?

key_points: To classify weathering, observe: (1) colour change? (2) texture change? (3) mineral identity change?
Physical → rock breaks but stays the same. Chemical → rock changes colour or texture. Biological → damage from organisms.
One rock can show all three types at once — the classification depends on which process you are describing.

key_vocabulary.example: Tree roots growing into rock crevices and gradually forcing the rock apart.
key_vocabulary.definition: The breakdown of rocks caused by the actions of living organisms, such as plant roots, lichens, and burrowing animals.

key_vocabulary.example: Water-filled cracks in granite rocks cracking apart after freezing overnight in cool mountain regions.
key_vocabulary.definition: Physical weathering caused by water entering cracks, freezing to expand, then thawing to contract, repeatedly stressing the rock.

common_mistakes: Assuming all pitting and damage is the same type of weathering (must examine the cause and what changed).
Overlooking biological weathering because it looks like just a crack (organism damage is real weathering).
educational_content.seychelles_context: On Seychelles mountains like Morne Blanc, you see all three types: freeze-thaw cracking (physical) on exposed peaks, iron oxidation staining (chemical) from tropical rains, and root widening of cracks (biological) from creeping vegetation in moist areas.

fields.teacher_script: Imagine you're sailing from Mahé to one of our outer islands in the Seychelles, or giving directions to a friend on a treasure map. fields.teacher_script: Look at the compass rose: the four main directions are North (N at 0°), East (E at 90°), South (S at 180°), and West (W at 270°)—these are called cardinal directions. Between them are the intercardinal directions: Northeast (NE at 45°), Southeast (SE at 135°), Southwest (SW at 225°), and Northwest (NW at 315°). A bearing is the angle you measure clockwise from North; for example, a bearing of 45° points Northeast, and a bearing of 270° points West. Think of it like the hand of a clock starting at 12 (North) and rotating clockwise to show your direction. Now, look at a map in front of you: can you identify which compass direction matches a bearing of 135°, and explain why that bearing points in that direction?

fields.teacher_script: Let's work through an example together. Suppose you're at Mahé Airport and you want to describe the direction to Praslin Island. If we say Praslin is to the Northeast (NE), what bearing in degrees would that be? Northeast is exactly halfway between North (0°) and East (90°), so the bearing is 45°. Now, if someone tells you a bearing of 225°, how do we convert that back to compass points? Start at North, rotate clockwise 225°. That's past South (180°) by 45°, which puts us at Southwest (SW). Notice: we always measure clockwise from North, and every compass point has an exact degree value.

fields.teacher_script: Now let's focus on biological weathering — weathering caused by living things. Look at the rock sample below. You can see a tree root wedged into a crack, lichen patches on the surface, and evidence of small animal burrows. Your task is to recognise which organisms are causing weathering and how. key_points: Tree roots and burrowing animals cause physical (mechanical) biological weathering by forcing rocks apart.

fields.teacher_script: In Seychelles, our granite islands are constantly shaped by the ocean, sun, and rain. Look at the rocks along Anse Royale beach — some have smooth, rounded surfaces while others show deep cracks and peeling layers. This is weathering: the breaking down of rocks over time. Today we'll explore three main types: physical, chemical, and biological. Let's start by asking: what's breaking these rocks apart on our islands?

key_points: Physical weathering breaks rocks apart mechanically without changing what they are made of.
Freeze-thaw occurs when water enters cracks, freezes and expands, then thaws and contracts.
Exfoliation is when outer layers of rock peel away due to temperature changes and pressure release.

key_vocabulary.example: Cracks in granite rocks on Seychelles beaches caused by daily temperature changes.
key_vocabulary.definition: The breaking down and wearing away of rocks by physical, chemical, or biological processes.

key_vocabulary.example: Freeze-thaw action cracking rocks apart, or exfoliation removing surface layers.
key_vocabulary.definition: The breakdown of rocks without changing their chemical composition, caused by mechanical forces.

common_mistakes: Thinking that physical weathering changes the rock's colour or composition (it doesn't — only size and shape change).
Confusing exfoliation with simply 'flaking off' — exfoliation is systematic layer-by-layer peeling.
educational_content.seychelles_context: Seychelles' granite peaks and coastal rocks experience daily temperature swings from tropical heat to cooler nights, driving freeze-thaw and exfoliation. This is why our beaches have so many rounded boulders and fractured rock outcrops.
